chapters.title: Chapter 5: Evaluating Startups and Building Your Portfolio

lessons.title: Case Study: A Bengaluru Professional Deploys Their First ₹10 Lakh in Startups

children.text: This final lesson puts the whole course into one story. Arnav Kulkarni is a 34-year-old senior product manager at a Bengaluru software company. They have watched colleagues make, and lose, money in startups, and decide to build a small angel portfolio properly. Over four years, Arnav sets a budget, finds deals, says no far more often than yes, handles the paperwork, deals with failures and a bridge-round request, uses reserves on a winner, and learns how to read a portfolio that is still mostly paper. Arnav and every company here are illustrative, but each decision uses a tool from an earlier chapter.

body.text: A good first angel portfolio is not measured by whether it finds a unicorn. It is measured by whether every decision followed a plan you could explain, so that the portfolio survives its failures and still owns its winners.

cells: Six-month emergency fund, term and health cover, no high-interest debt, retirement SIPs running
₹1.2 crore, mostly equity mutual funds and FDs
₹10 lakh over three years, about 8.3% of investable net worth
30%, or ₹3 lakh, held back for follow-ons
₹7 lakh across 7 companies at ₹1 lakh each, the minimum on the syndicates Arnav uses
Not accredited, so new SEBI angel funds are closed; uses syndicates offering direct allotment, plus occasional direct deals
48-hour cooling-off period; no cheque without documents; reserves only for winners

body.text: Arnav is honest about the trade-off. Seven companies is fewer than the 15 to 25 often recommended. At an illustrative 3% chance of a big winner per company, the chance of owning at least one is only about 19%. Arnav accepts this because a ₹1 lakh minimum and a ₹10 lakh budget leave no better option, and plans to add companies only as the budget grows, not by stretching it.

children.text: Stage 2: Year 1, Finding and Filtering Deals

In the first year, Arnav sees 42 startups through two syndicates and a local founder meet-up. Most are rejected after a quick look at the deck. Six get a full evaluation using the four-pillar scorecard from Chapter 5, Lesson 1.

body.caption: The six deals Arnav evaluated in Year 1 (scores out of 5)

cells: LedgerLoop: practice software for CA firms
Invested ₹1 lakh in CCPS at ₹18 crore post-money; strong retention, clear expansion path
Passed; LTV to CAC of 1.6x and growth dependent on discounts
Passed; capital-heavy lending model with regulatory complexity Arnav could not judge
ScanSetu: diagnostics marketplace for Tier-2 cities
Invested ₹1 lakh through an iSAFE with a ₹25 crore cap and 20% discount
ResumeRocket: AI CV tool, founded by a friend
Passed politely; market too small and crowded, despite the friendship
FarmFresh Grid: cold-chain for farmer groups
Invested ₹1 lakh in equity shares at ₹12 crore post-money, directly

body.title: Arnav's LedgerLoop stake
body.prompt: Arnav invests ₹1 lakh in LedgerLoop at an ₹18 crore post-money valuation. What percentage of the company does Arnav own? Give your answer to three decimal places.
body.explanation: ₹1 lakh ÷ ₹18 crore = ₹1 lakh ÷ ₹1,800 lakh = 0.000556, or about 0.056%. Tiny percentages are normal for small angel cheques; what matters is whether the company can grow large enough for that slice to be worth a great deal.

children.text: For each investment, Arnav keeps a folder: signed agreements, the PAS-4 offer letter, the bank transfer to the company, and a screenshot of the PAS-3 filing on the MCA portal. FarmFresh Grid's PAS-3 had not appeared after the 60-day allotment window. A polite follow-up revealed the company secretary had missed the deadline; it was filed with late fees within two weeks. Small lapses like this are common, but checking caught it.
Stage 3: Years 2 and 3, Completing the Portfolio

events.title: Three cheques
events.description: LedgerLoop, ScanSetu and FarmFresh Grid, ₹1 lakh each.

events.title: Two more, and one mistake
events.description: Adds two startups. One, a creator-economy app called ClipCart, is backed within 24 hours of a demo day pitch, breaking Arnav's own cooling-off rule.

events.title: Portfolio complete
events.description: Adds two final companies, reaching 7 companies and ₹7 lakh invested. One early company shuts down.

events.title: Bridge request declined
events.description: ClipCart asks for more money with 3 months of runway and worsening unit economics. Arnav declines; reserves are for winners.

events.title: A winner and an exit
events.description: LedgerLoop raises a Series A at a much higher valuation; Arnav uses ₹1.5 lakh of reserves. FarmFresh Grid is acquired for about 1.8x Arnav's cost. A second company shuts down.

body.title: The bridge decision
body.question: ClipCart, the company Arnav backed in a rush, asks for a bridge investment. It has 3 months of runway and losses per order are rising. Arnav has ₹3 lakh of unused reserves. What is the most disciplined response?
options: Invest the full ₹3 lakh to protect the original ₹1 lakh
Decline, unless verifiable evidence shows it is a strong new investment on its own merits
Demand that the founder repay the original ₹1 lakh
body.explanation: Reserves are for companies pulling ahead, not rescues. Investing to protect the first cheque is the sunk cost fallacy. Equity investors also have no right to demand repayment. Declining is not disloyal; it protects the reserves for a company that has earned them.

children.text: Stage 4: Reading the Portfolio After Four Years

markDefs.definition: Total Value to Paid-In: cash received plus the current estimated value of remaining holdings, divided by total money invested.
Distributions to Paid-In: cash actually received back, divided by total money invested. It ignores paper value.

children.text: By the end of Year 4, Arnav has invested ₹8.5 lakh: ₹7 lakh in initial cheques plus ₹1.5 lakh of follow-on. Two numbers describe the portfolio honestly.

body.caption: Arnav's portfolio at the end of Year 4 (values are illustrative estimates)

cells: Series A at a higher valuation; stake valued at 5x after dilution
Bought at the Series A price
Acquired: 80% paid at closing, 20% in escrow
₹1.8 lakh, of which ₹1.44 lakh received in cash
Growing slowly; iSAFE not yet converted
₹9.8 lakh, of which ₹1.44 lakh in cash

body.latex: \text{TVPI} = \frac{\text{Cash received} + \text{Current value of holdings}}{\text{Total invested}} \qquad \text{DPI} = \frac{\text{Cash received}}{\text{Total invested}}
body.caption: Escrow still owed is counted in current value, not in cash received, until it is actually paid out.

body.title: Calculate Arnav's TVPI
body.prompt: Arnav has invested ₹8.5 lakh. Cash received plus the current estimated value of all holdings, including escrow still due, totals ₹9.8 lakh. What is Arnav's TVPI? Give your answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: TVPI = ₹9.8 lakh ÷ ₹8.5 lakh = 1.153, or about 1.15x. DPI = ₹1.44 lakh ÷ ₹8.5 lakh = 0.17x. On paper Arnav is slightly ahead after four years; in cash, only 17% of the money has come back so far. Both numbers are normal at this stage.

body.title: Arnav's 7 companies by status after four years

body.text: Angel portfolios usually look worst in the early years: failures arrive fast, while winners take longer to show up. Investors call this the J-curve. Arnav's result will be decided almost entirely by LedgerLoop, exactly as the power law predicts. The paper marks are also estimates; ₹5 lakh becomes real only if LedgerLoop keeps growing and an exit actually happens.

children.text: The FarmFresh Grid shares were unlisted and held for about three years, so the ₹80,000 gain on the ₹1.8 lakh sale is long-term. On its own, it would be taxed at 12.5%, or ₹10,000 before surcharge and cess. But Arnav also has ₹2 lakh of long-term capital losses from the two shutdowns, which were formally wound up after more than 24 months. Those losses can be set off against the gain.

body.caption: Arnav's capital gains position (illustrative; timing of escrow tax treated as confirmed by a chartered accountant)

cells: Long-term gain on FarmFresh Grid (₹1.8 lakh − ₹1 lakh)
Long-term losses from two wound-up companies
Long-term loss carried forward, if the return is filed on time

body.label: Why record-keeping paid off
body.value: ₹1.2 lakh of losses available for future gains
body.context: Because Arnav kept wind-up documents and filed the tax return on time, the unused losses can offset long-term gains, perhaps from LedgerLoop, for up to eight years.

columns.label: What worked
points: A fixed budget and reserves, set before the first deal
Passing on five of six fully evaluated deals in Year 1, including a friend's
Checking PAS-3 filings and keeping complete records
Declining the ClipCart bridge and using reserves on LedgerLoop instead

columns.label: What Arnav would change
points: Never break the cooling-off rule; ClipCart was the only rushed deal and the only avoidable loss
Negotiate pro-rata rights on every deal, not just some
Spread initial cheques more evenly across years
Grow the number of companies as the budget allows, to reduce luck-dependence

body.title: Arnav's Year 5 decision
body.scenario: In Year 5, LedgerLoop raises a Series B at three times its Series A price. Arnav's pro-rata right would require ₹4 lakh, but only ₹1.5 lakh of reserves remain. At the same time, a growth fund in the round offers to buy half of Arnav's LedgerLoop shares at the Series B price. LedgerLoop is now the only company carrying the portfolio.
body.prompt: What options does Arnav have, and how should they think it through?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Arnav should not stretch the plan to find the full ₹4 lakh. The budget was set for good reasons, and topping it up because one company is doing well is overconfidence dressed as conviction.
2. Option A: invest the remaining ₹1.5 lakh of reserves in the Series B. This keeps part of the pro-rata position in the portfolio's clear winner, which is exactly what reserves are for.
3. Option B: sell half the existing shares to the growth fund. At three times the Series A price, the initial stake valued at ₹5 lakh and the follow-on at ₹1.5 lakh would be worth roughly ₹19.5 lakh on paper, so selling half would return close to ₹10 lakh in cash, more than the entire ₹8.5 lakh invested so far, while keeping the other half of the upside.
4. Options A and B can be combined: using reserves while selling part of the older stake is a coherent power-law strategy, locking in the portfolio's cost while keeping meaningful exposure.
5. Before deciding, Arnav should check the shareholders' agreement for transfer restrictions or a right of first refusal, understand the tax on the sale, confirm the growth fund's offer in writing, and review how large LedgerLoop has become relative to Arnav's overall net worth.

body.title: Name the metric
body.textWithBlank: A ratio that counts only cash actually returned to investors, divided by total money invested, is called distributions to ___-in, or DPI.
body.explanation: DPI is distributions to paid-in capital. Unlike TVPI, it ignores paper valuations, which makes it the harder, more honest test of whether an angel portfolio has actually made money.

body.title: Your own first-portfolio plan
steps: Complete the readiness checklist from Chapter 5, Lesson 2.
Calculate your investable net worth and set a total angel budget.
Choose your reserve percentage and target number of companies, and work out your initial cheque size.
Decide which routes are open to you: direct deals, syndicates or, if accredited, SEBI angel funds.
Write down your personal rules, including a cooling-off period and a no-documents, no-cheque rule.
Prepare your four-pillar scorecard and a list of diligence questions.
Set up a record-keeping folder and speak to a chartered accountant before your first investment.
Commit to reviewing the portfolio once a year using TVPI and DPI.

cards.definition: Total Value to Paid-In: cash received plus current value of holdings, divided by total invested.
Distributions to Paid-In: cash actually received, divided by total invested.
An estimated value of unlisted holdings, usually based on the latest round price, which is not cash until an exit.
The pattern where angel and venture portfolios look worst early, as failures come before winners.
The narrowing from deals seen, to founder calls, to full evaluations, to investments.
Reducing the estimated value of a holding that is struggling, before any formal write-off.
Selling part of a winning stake to lock in gains while keeping some upside.

points: Set the budget, reserves, number of companies and personal rules before seeing a single deal, and write down the trade-offs you are accepting.
Expect to say no to most deals, including ones from friends; a scorecard makes that easier and more consistent.
Paperwork and record-keeping protect you twice: when you invest, and when you use losses against gains at tax time.
Use reserves only for companies pulling ahead, and decline bridge rounds that would only rescue a past decision.
Read your portfolio with both TVPI and DPI; early years usually look weak on cash, and one winner tends to decide the result.
When a winner dominates, combine follow-on investment and partial secondary sales rather than breaking your budget.
